# Tasks

## Task 1-3: Data Acquisition, Cleaning & Preparation
```{r}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
#Task 1: Data Acquisition
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event)
}

# Task 2: Fix Column Titles
NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()

NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  rename(
    title = Title,
    runtime = Runtime,
    views = Views,
    hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
    release_date = `Release Date`,
    available_globally = `Available Globally?`
  )

#Task 3: Fix Column Types
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),
    available_globally = available_globally == "Yes"
  )

```

## Task 5: Exploratory Questions - Inline Values

### Question 1: What date range is covered by this data set?

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    earliest_period = min(period_start),
    latest_period = max(period_end)
  )
```
The date range  covered by this data set is **January 1, 2023 (2023-01-01) to July 30, 2026 (2026-07-30)**.

### Question 2: How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set?

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    distinct_titles = n_distinct(title)
  )
```
There are **24,427** different shows and movies covered in this data set. 

### Question 3: How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the *Bridgerton* universe?

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours_viewed_bridgerton = sum(hours_viewed)
  )
```
A total of **4,862,800,000** hours have been spent watching shows from the *Bridgerton* universe. 

### Question 4:How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things?

```{r}
# For this question, we only want the “real” *Stranger Things* shows and not the companion behind-the-scenes show (“Beyond Stranger Things”), the animated spin-off (“Tales from ’85”), or the background music (“Stranger Things: Fireplace”).

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Fireplace")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales From")) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )
```

A total of **5,548,500,000** hours have been spent watching the five seasons of *Stranger Things* excluding the BTS, spin-off and background music.

### Question 5: What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?

> Step 1: Calculate total watch time in 2026H1
```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  summarise(
    total_2026h1_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )
```

> Step 2: Identify the Top 10 titles based on total views in 2026 H1
```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    total_views = sum(views, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_views)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

> Step 3: Calculate total hours viewed for the Top 10 titles

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  filter(title %in% c(
    "His & Hers: Limited Series",
    "Bridgerton: Season 4",
    "I Will Find You: Limited Series",
    "Stranger Things 5",
    "Run Away: Limited Series",
    "Teach You a Lesson: Limited Series",
    "ONE PIECE: Season 2",
    "Man on Fire: Season 1",
    "Ms. Rachel: Season 1",
    "The Night Agent: Season 3"
  )) |>
  summarise(
    top_10_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )

```

> Final step is the calculation: top_10_hours_viewed / total_2026h1_hours_viewed * 100 = (4138400000 / 74333600000) * 100) =  5.57%

The Top 10 titles accounted for **`r sprintf("%.2f%%", (4138400000 / 74333600000) * 100)`** of total viewing time.


### Question 6: What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available? (Answer this both by title and weighted by hours viewed)

> Part 1: Calculate Netflix’s catalog globally available by title

```{r}
# Step 1: Calculate Netflix’s total available titles (we already calculated this in Q2)

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    distinct_titles = n_distinct(title)
  )

# Step 2: Calculate Netflix’s total globally available titles
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(available_globally == TRUE) |>
  summarise(
    titles_available_globally = n_distinct(title, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```

> Final step is calculation: Fraction of Netflix’s globally available catalog by hours viewed is globally_available_hours_viewed / total_hours_viewed * 100 = (265637100000 / 511590500000) * 100) = 24.60%



> Part 2: Calculate Netflix’s catalog globally available weighted by hours viewed

```{r}
# Step 1: Calculate Netflix’s total hours viewed
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    total_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )

# Step 2: Calculate total hours viewed for titles available globally

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(available_globally == TRUE) |>
  summarise(
    globally_available_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)
  )

```

> Final step is calculation: Fraction of Netflix’s globally available catalog by hours viewed is globally_available_hours_viewed / total_hours_viewed * 100 = (265637100000 / 511590500000) * 100) = 51.92%

Fraction of Netflix’s globally available catalog by title is **`r sprintf("%.2f%%", (6010 / 24427) * 100)`** and weighted by hours viewed is **`r sprintf("%.2f%%", (265637100000 / 511590500000) * 100)`**


## Task 6: Exploratory Questions - Table Answers

### Question 1: What was the top show (by total hours viewed) in each period and what fraction of total viewership did it capture?

```{r}

library(dplyr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Compute the top show and its share per period
top_shows_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>

  # Aggregate hours viewed by period and title (in case titles appear multiple times in a period)
  group_by(period, title) |>
  summarise(
    hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), 
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Group by period alone to calculate the period total and fraction
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    period_total = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    fraction = hours_viewed / period_total
  ) |>
  # Isolate the row with the maximum hours viewed for each period
  slice_max(order_by = hours_viewed, n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

# Step 2: Format and display using gt for your memo
top_shows_by_period |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, fraction) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = hours_viewed,
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = fraction,
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = md("**Reporting Period**"),
    title = md("**Top Show**"),
    hours_viewed = md("**Total Hours Viewed**"),
    fraction = md("**Fraction of Viewership**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Top Netflix Show by Period**"),
    subtitle = md("*Peak Viewership Analysis*")
  )

```

**Wednesday: Season 2 ** was the *top performing show in 2025H2*, attracting **964.1 million hours** viewed and capturing **1.35% of total viewership**. The result suggests that Wednesday: Season 2 had the strongest relative performance compared with other titles in its reporting period. Additionally, it has the highest viewership share among all the top shows across the seven reporting periods.

### Question 2: How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.

```{r}
# Step 1: Summarize catalog size by period
catalog_evolution <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period, period_start) |>  # including period_start to keep data chronologically sorted
  summarise(
    total_titles = n_distinct(title),
    total_runtime = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(period_start) # Sort chronologically

# Step 2: Format using gt
catalog_evolution |>
  select(period, total_titles, total_runtime) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles, total_runtime),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = md("**Period**"),
    total_titles = md("**Number of Titles**"),
    total_runtime = md("**Total Runtime**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Evolution of Netflix Catalog Size**"),
    subtitle = md("*Tracking Title Count and Total Runtime Across Reporting Periods*")
  )
```

Netflix had the highest number of titles but the lowest total runtime in the first half of 2023. In the second half of the year, the number of titles dropped significantly, while total runtime increased. In the following periods, both the number of titles and total runtime gradually increased. This suggests that Netflix’s catalog became smaller but the viewrship improved in the second half of 2023. The increase in runtime despite having fewer titles may also indicate a shift toward longer content or titles that attracted more viewing. 

### Question 3: Which shows have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods?

version 1

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Clean show titles and aggregate performance across periods
staples_high_floor <- NETFLIX_DATA %>%
  mutate(
    show_name = str_replace(
      title, 
      regex("([:\\s\\-]+)?(season|volume|part|limited series).*$", ignore_case = TRUE), 
      ""
    ),
    show_name = str_trim(show_name)
  ) %>%
  group_by(show_name, period) %>%
  summarise(
    period_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop_last"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    periods_present = n_distinct(period),
    mean_hours = mean(period_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_hours = min(period_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_hours = max(period_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_hours = sd(period_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Step 2: Filter for presence across 5+ periods and sort by MINIMUM floor
  filter(
    periods_present >= 5,
    mean_hours >= 50000000,
    min_hours >= 10000000
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(min_hours)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

# Step 3: Format and display using gt
staples_high_floor %>%
  select(show_name, periods_present, min_hours, mean_hours, max_hours, sd_hours) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(min_hours, mean_hours, max_hours, sd_hours),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    show_name = "Show / Franchise Name",
    periods_present = "Periods Active",
    min_hours = "Min Hours (Floor)",
    mean_hours = "Mean Hours",
    max_hours = "Max Hours",
    sd_hours = "Std. Deviation"
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Top 5 'Staple' Franchises Ranked by Viewership Floor",
    subtitle = "Highest Guaranteed Baseline Performance (Min Hours Across 5+ Periods)"
  )
```

### Question 4: Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?

``` {r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Create the content type classification heuristic
classified_netflix <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    # Heuristic: Classify as TV Show or Movie based on title text and runtime
    content_type = case_when(
      str_detect(title, regex("season|limited series|volume|part", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "TV Show",
      runtime > 240 ~ "TV Show", # Anything over 4 hours total runtime is a show
      TRUE ~ "Movie"             # Default everything else to Movie
    )
  )

# Step 2: Aggregate hours viewed by period and content type
period_content_split <- classified_netflix |>
  group_by(period, period_start, content_type) |>
  summarise(
    hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Calculate the fraction of total viewership for each content type per period
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(
    period_total = sum(hours_viewed),
    fraction = hours_viewed / period_total
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(period_start)

# Step 3: Format and display using gt (Pivot wider for a clean comparison table)
period_content_split |>
  select(period, content_type, fraction) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = content_type,
    values_from = fraction
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(`TV Show`, Movie),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = md("**Reporting Period**"),
    `TV Show` = md("**TV Shows (%)**"),
    Movie = md("**Movies (%)**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Viewership Share: TV Shows vs. Movies**"),
    subtitle = md("*Estimated via Heuristic (Title Keywords & Runtime Thresholds)*")
  )
```
Within each period, the fraction of time spent on shows is significantly higher than movies. The time spent on movies in the first half of 2023, although, still lower than shows was relatively higher than the time spent on movies in rest of the time periods. However, this number noticeably dropped for the rest of the time periods. This indicates that shows dominated viewership by a huge margin throughout all given time periods. 

### Queston 5: How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Summarize viewership metrics comparing live events vs. pre-taped content
live_comparison <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(live_event) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles = n(),
    mean_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90_hours = quantile(hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE), # Top tier (90th percentile)
    max_hours = max(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),           # Absolute peak / breakout hit
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(live_event, "Live Events", "Pre-Taped Content")
  )

# Step 2: Format and display using gt for your memo
live_comparison |>
  select(content_type, total_titles, mean_hours, median_hours, p90_hours, max_hours) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles, mean_hours, median_hours, p90_hours, max_hours),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    content_type = "Content Type",
    total_titles = md("**Total Count**"),
    mean_hours = md("**Average Hours Viewed**"),
    median_hours = md("**Median Hours Viewed**"),
    p90_hours = md("**Top Tier (90th Percentile)**"),
    max_hours = md("**Maximum (Peak Hit)**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content Performance**"),
    subtitle = md("*Comparing Average and Top-Tier Viewership*")
  )

```

Pre-taped content averages 8.29 million viewing hours, more than double the 3.56 million hours for live events. However, the median viewing hours are very similar - 1.8 million for pre-taped content and 1.7 million for live events. This suggests that while a few highly popular pre-taped titles raise the average, typical titles in both categories perform similarly.

Pre-taped content performs better at the high end. At the 90th percentile, pre-taped titles reach 20 million viewing hours, compared to 6.5 million for live events. The most-viewed pre-taped title also reached 964.1 million hours (which from our previous analysis, we know is Wednesday: Season 2), nearly four times the 235.7 million hours of the top live event. This suggests that pre-taped content has greater potential to attract very large audiences.

adding on to it:

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Compute total platform metrics for proportion baselines
total_platform_titles <- nrow(NETFLIX_DATA)
total_platform_hours  <- sum(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 2: Calculate aggregate performance, total viewership, and efficiency metrics
live_efficiency_summary <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(live_event) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles = n(),
    catalog_share = n() / total_platform_titles,
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), # Total viewership hours
    viewership_share = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) / total_platform_hours,
    
    # Efficiency Metrics
    yield_per_title = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 
    efficiency_index = (sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) / total_platform_hours) / (n() / total_platform_titles),
    
    # Benchmarks
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90_hours = quantile(hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_hours = max(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(live_event, "Live Events", "Pre-Taped Content")
  )

# Step 3: Display in a publication-quality gt table including total hours
live_efficiency_summary |>
  select(
    content_type, total_titles, catalog_share, total_hours, viewership_share, 
    efficiency_index, median_hours, p90_hours, max_hours
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(total_titles, total_hours, median_hours, p90_hours, max_hours),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(catalog_share, viewership_share),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(efficiency_index),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    content_type = "Content Type",
    total_titles = md("**Catalog Count**"),
    catalog_share = md("**Catalog Share (%)**"),
    total_hours = md("**Total Viewership Hours**"),
    viewership_share = md("**Viewership Share (%)**"),
    efficiency_index = md("**Efficiency Index**"),
    median_hours = md("**Median Hours**"),
    p90_hours = md("**Top Tier (90th Pctl)**"),
    max_hours = md("**Peak Hit**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content: Scale & Efficiency**"),
    subtitle = md("*Evaluating Catalog Footprint, Total Viewership, and Efficiency Distribution*")
  )
```

# Step 1: Global Data Cleaning & Classification
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>

  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex(
          "season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|vs\\.|show|live|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", 
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

clean_total_titles <- nrow(cleaned_netflix_data)
clean_total_hours  <- sum(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 2: Summarise Portfolio Matrix Data

  summarise(
    catalog_share    = n() / clean_total_titles,
    viewership_share = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE) / clean_total_hours,
    efficiency_index = viewership_share / catalog_share,

  )

deeper analysis:


```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Clean dataset
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex(
          "season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|vs\\.|show|live|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order",
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      ),
      "TV Shows", "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Calculate percentile thresholds
p90_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
p75_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
p25_clean <- quantile(cleaned_netflix_data$hours_viewed, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Summarise performance per segment
hit_rate_summary <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(
    total_titles     = n(),
    top_tier_pct     = mean(hours_viewed >= p90_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    strong_pct       = mean(hours_viewed >= p75_clean & hours_viewed < p90_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    moderate_pct     = mean(hours_viewed >= p25_clean & hours_viewed < p75_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    underperform_pct = mean(hours_viewed < p25_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(top_tier_pct))

# Step 4: GT Table
exec_hit_rate_matrix <- hit_rate_summary |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(total_titles), use_seps = TRUE, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(top_tier_pct, strong_pct, moderate_pct, underperform_pct), decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(
    segment          = md("**Strategic Segment**"),
    total_titles     = md("**Total Titles**"),
    top_tier_pct     = md("**Top Tier Hits (>=P90)**"),
    strong_pct       = md("**Strong (P75–P90)**"),
    moderate_pct     = md("**Moderate (P25–P75)**"),
    underperform_pct = md("**Underperforming (<P25)**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title    = md("**Netflix Portfolio Performance**"),
    subtitle = md("*Share of Titles by Viewership Performance*")
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    heading.title.font.size = px(18),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  )

# Display Table
exec_hit_rate_matrix

```



best titles and performance for each segment:

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(gt)

# Step 1: Clean and standardize NETFLIX_DATA
cleaned_netflix_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!str_detect(title, regex("other shows|aggregate|summary|total", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(
    content_type = if_else(
      str_detect(
        title, 
        regex(
          "season|volume|part|series|limited series|episode|s[0-9]|year|vs\\.|show|live|chiquititas|mr\\. queen|law & order", 
          ignore_case = TRUE
        )
      ),
      "TV Shows", 
      "Movies"
    ),
    availability_type = if_else(
      available_globally %in% c(TRUE, "Yes", "TRUE", 1),
      "Global", "Regional"
    ),
    segment = paste(availability_type, content_type)
  )

# Step 2: Extract Top 10 Best Performing titles per segment
top_10_per_segment <- cleaned_netflix_data |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  slice_max(order_by = hours_viewed, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  select(segment, rank, title, hours_viewed) |>
  ungroup()

# Step 3: Render GT Table
top_10_per_segment |>
  gt(groupname_col = "segment") |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(hours_viewed),
    use_seps = TRUE,
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    rank = md("**Rank**"),
    title = md("**Title**"),
    hours_viewed = md("**Hours Viewed**")
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Top 10 Best Performing Titles**"),
    subtitle = md("*Categorized by Segment*")
  )
```
